title: Evaluating Generate–Validate–Repair Pipelines for Intent‑to‑Configuration NetOps Tasks: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study comparing a baseline single‑shot LLM configuration generator against a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline (with a canary stage) on a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus (2000 paired episodes). The declared model was gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses) and validation used a deterministic digital‑twin validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics exactly one sampled initial generation per task was deterministically reused by both arms; downstream validation and the permitted single repair call (guarded arm only) were the only mechanisms for paired outcome differences. Observed outcomes: baseline safe‑deploy = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded safe‑deploy = 1000/1000 = 1.000; paired difference = 0.005 (n11=995, n10=5, n01=0, n00=0). The preregistered primary inferential test (exact two‑sided McNemar) yields p = 0.0625 (not < 0.05). The preregistered secondary descriptive summary (paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI, 10,000 resamples, seed 1729) is [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred and total model calls used = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5). We present the exact McNemar result as the preregistered confirmatory outcome, report the bootstrap CI as a descriptive summary, explicitly label any one‑sided McNemar as exploratory (not prespecified), and interpret the small absolute guarded benefit in light of sparse discordant counts, high baseline validity, validator scope, and the shared_initial_candidate design.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation for network operations promises reduced manual effort but carries safety risks: sequencing errors, transient invariant violations, and protected‑field interference can convert plausible command sequences into harmful actions. Prior surveys and controlled studies document LLM hallucination, prompt sensitivity, and structured‑output failures that affect code and configuration generation, motivating architectures that pair generative models with deterministic validators and bounded repair procedures [1],[2].

This paper reports a preregistered, artifact‑grounded paired experiment (cand‑003‑stud‑001) that isolates purely downstream validator/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Our research question is: when baseline and guarded conditions begin from the exact same sampled initial candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics), to what degree can a downstream deterministic validator plus a single allowed repair call (guarded pipeline with a canary stage) improve paired safe‑deploy outcomes compared with reusing the same initial candidate unmodified (baseline)? The design intentionally isolates downstream interventions so that any paired difference is attributable to those downstream mechanisms rather than to first‑pass generation differences such as prompt engineering, constrained decoding, or sampling variance.

Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired experiment (Npairs = 1000) with deterministic task selection from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 corpus and archived validator traces. (2) Full execution accounting: completed pairs = 1000; total hosted model calls recorded = 1005 (shared_initial = 1000; repair = 5); repair invocations = 5. (3) Transparent inferential reporting: the preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the confirmatory test (p = 0.0625) and is not significant at two‑sided α = 0.05; preregistered bootstrap summaries and any post‑hoc directional tests are labeled descriptive/exploratory.
sections.related_work:
Surveys and controlled analyses show that LLMs suffer from hallucination and prompt sensitivity that materially affect correctness for code and structured outputs; these findings motivate verifier‑assisted repair and guarded architectures in NetOps contexts [1],[2]. Work on constrained decoding and schema‑aware planning demonstrates reductions in syntactic/executable errors in structured domains, though many demonstrations come from non‑NetOps areas and their transfer depends on validator fidelity [3]. Recent NetOps and agentic‑AI system papers propose verifier‑assisted repair, protocol‑mediated execution, and audit/proof mechanisms to reduce automation risk; these works provide prototypes and architectural arguments emphasizing validator coverage and governance rather than model changes alone [4],[5],[6].

Our study complements this literature by preregistering a paired comparison that isolates the incremental effect of deterministic downstream validation and a single limited repair call when the initial candidate is held constant across conditions, avoiding conflation with first‑pass generation interventions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistration (cand‑003‑stud‑001) was frozen prior to any hosted‑model invocation (preregistration_sha256 recorded in the manifest = ab4c6436c6ece56bf47da7730d50485a17cdb9bb86a90a4231042303d3b489ec). Key preregistered elements: paired binary design; task_count = 1000 deterministically drawn from the challenging_workflow_stress_v1 synthetic corpus; generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one sampled initial generation reused by both conditions); initial_generation_calls_per_task = 1; maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1; primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact two‑sided McNemar. Secondary preregistered summaries: paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729) and sensitivity analyses treating failed calls as unsafe.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics. Because both arms begin from the exact same sampled candidate, any paired difference can arise only from deterministic validator decisions and the permitted single repair call; the design therefore isolates downstream interventions and does not measure effects from independent first‑pass generation differences or prompt‑engineering arms not executed.

Model and validator configuration. The declared model in the execution manifest is gpt‑5‑mini (provider: openai_responses). The archived model_configuration.json records temperature = null/unset; null/unset is not evidence of deterministic hosted‑model sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. The orchestration adapter was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and validation used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator version 5.0). The validator enforces workflow policies, required command presence and order, protected‑field noninterference, and returns a deterministic binary safe‑deploy verdict per task manifest.

Task corpus and scoring. Tasks include initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty labels (very_hard, extreme). The validator compares parsed candidate command sequences against manifest constraints in a deterministic digital‑twin emulator and emits structured validator traces archived per episode. Scoring used scoring_rule = full_intent_constraint_validation producing a binary validity outcome required by the paired analysis.

Execution controls and missingness. The preregistration limited retries (maximum_attempts_per_call = 1) and prespecified missingness treatments (primary: complete_pair_primary). Seeds and deterministic task selection rules were fixed before model calls. All retries, failures, and adapter events were recorded in the execution manifest and deterministic reconciliation artifacts.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The execution manifest records start 2026‑09‑01T06:31:07Z, completion 2026‑09‑01T08:38:57Z, planned episodes = 2000, completed episodes = 2000, complete_pairs = 1000, failed episodes = 0. Provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 1005, stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation = 1000, repair = 5}, and cache_miss_count = 1005; all deterministic consistency checks passed.

Primary paired outcomes and preregistered inferential test. The 2×2 contingency table is: n11 = 995 (both succeeded), n10 = 5 (guarded succeeded, baseline failed), n01 = 0 (baseline succeeded, guarded failed), n00 = 0 (both failed). Observed success rates: baseline = 995/1000 = 0.995; guarded = 1000/1000 = 1.000; observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.005. The preregistered confirmatory test (exact two‑sided McNemar) returns p = 0.0625; preregistered H1 is not supported at two‑sided α = 0.05.

Preregistered secondary descriptive summaries and repair diagnostics. The preregistered paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) yields [0.001, 0.01]. Only five validator‑triggered repairs occurred; representative episode artifacts show the validator rejecting initial candidates for required_sequence or protected_interface violations, the adapter invoking the permitted single repair call, and the validator accepting the repaired candidate upon revalidation. All raw responses, provider call traces, repair traces (where present), and validator traces are archived and referenced in the execution artifacts.
sections.discussion:
Confirmatory vs descriptive hierarchy (REVISED per reviewer). The preregistered exact two‑sided McNemar is the study's confirmatory analysis and it did not reach two‑sided α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625); this is the primary inferential conclusion. The paired bootstrap percentile CI ([0.001, 0.01]) and any directional one‑sided McNemar reported elsewhere are preregistered descriptive or post‑hoc/exploratory summaries and do not overturn the preregistered confirmatory null. The bootstrap CI can exclude zero here because bootstrap percentile intervals are sensitive when discordant counts are extremely sparse (n10 + n01 small); resampling discrete paired outcomes with only five discordant pairs can produce nonzero percentile bounds even when the exact paired test yields a nondiscoverable two‑sided p‑value.

Interpretive synthesis and threats to validity. The shared_initial_candidate design proves that observed paired differences derive from validator decisions and permitted repairs only. The observed small absolute improvement (0.005) must be read against three constraints: (1) extremely high baseline validity (0.995) reduces discordant pairs and thus power for the preregistered exact paired test (the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target absolute effect of 0.15), (2) only five repairs were invoked, limiting inference about repair efficacy across failure classes, and (3) construct validity depends on deterministic_netops_validator_v5 rule coverage—unmodeled semantic or emergent multi‑device policy errors would not be detected. External validity is limited by the single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini) and the synthetic corpus.
sections.conclusion: In a preregistered paired study using shared_initial_candidate semantics over a 1000‑task synthetic NetOps stress corpus, a guarded generate→validate→repair pipeline produced a small absolute paired improvement (0.005) relative to a baseline single‑shot generator; the preregistered two‑sided McNemar test did not reach α = 0.05 (p = 0.0625). Five validator repairs were invoked and total model calls recorded = 1005. These artifact‑grounded results indicate that downstream verifier/repair safeguards can avert some unsafe outcomes in synthetic workflows, but measurable marginal gains depend strongly on baseline failure prevalence, validator sensitivity/coverage, and repair budget. We release archived preregistration, execution manifests, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to enable preregistered follow‑ups that vary generator semantics, repair budgets, validator rule sets, and model families.

limitations: Single‑model scope: only the declared model gpt‑5‑mini was evaluated; results do not generalize across model families or versions.

Synthetic corpus and deterministic validator: tasks come from a synthetic stress corpus and validation used a deterministic digital twin (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); external validity to heterogeneous vendor/legacy environments is limited.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired comparison isolates downstream validator/repair effects only; it does not measure differences that would arise from independent first‑pass generations or alternative prompting arms that were not executed (those arms were not part of the frozen preregistration).

Low baseline failure prevalence: baseline success = 99.5%; the preregistered power plan assumed baseline≈0.60 and a target effect of 0.15, so the observed baseline greatly reduces sensitivity to detect small absolute gains. This mismatch is reported explicitly and reduces the study's ability to detect very small practical effects using the preregistered confirmatory test.
Sparse repairs and interpretation limits: only five validator repairs were invoked, constraining inference about repair efficacy across failure modes.

Statistical nuance: the preregistered primary test is exact two‑sided McNemar (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap percentile CI [0.001, 0.01] is a preregistered descriptive summary but is sensitive to sparse discordant counts; a one‑sided McNemar (p = 0.03125) was computed post‑hoc and is explicitly labeled exploratory because it was not prespecified in the frozen preregistration.

Construct validity: the safe‑deploy binary depends on the emulator/validator's rule set; semantic and emergent multi‑device policy violations may be underrepresented in the validator's modeled constraints.
